title: He who is (ST I.13.11)
hook: the best name for God is he who is, being itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, analogy: our words for God are true, and too small. Your line was like, and more.

A shepherd stands barefoot on a mountainside in front of a bush that burns and is not burned up. A voice has just told him to go back to Egypt and bring his people out. Moses has a practical worry. When I tell them the God of their fathers sent me, they'll ask his name. What do I say? The answer is a name that's barely a name at all. You first stood at this bush on day two hundred ninety-five. Now Thomas Aquinas asks which name for God fits best. Today's word is that name.
screen: `A BUSH THAT ISN'T BURNED UP.` → `WHAT IS HIS NAME?` → `A NAME THAT'S BARELY A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here is God's answer to Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." And then: "Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." Thomas asks whether He who is is the most fitting name for God. Yes, he says, for three reasons. First, what it means. Every other name names a kind of thing, or a quality. Rock. Shepherd. Wise. Good. This one names no kind at all. It names to be. And two days ago, Thomas said that in God, what God is and that God is are one. So a name that means simply is fits as no other does. Second, how open it is. Other names narrow God to one side; this one sets no edge. Thomas quotes an earlier teacher, John Damascene: this name holds being itself like a sea without limit or bound. Remember the girl who couldn't see the other side. Third, the tense. Not he who was. Not he who will be. He who is. Following Augustine, Thomas says there is no past or future in God. The name is always now. Then, careful as ever, a turn. In another respect, he says, the name God, and the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible, are more proper still, because they name God alone. No single name holds God; each catches something. That's analogy, carried all the way. But Thomas keeps a special place for this one: the name that points not at something God has, but at what God is.
screen: `I AM WHO AM.` · `NOT A KIND OF THING: TO BE.` · `A SEA WITHOUT LIMIT.` · `ALWAYS NOW, NEVER WAS.` · then, large: `HE WHO IS, HATH SENT ME TO YOU.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say two words slowly under your breath, God is, adding nothing, let them go quiet, then say them again on the next breath. If you don't pray, try the smallest word of all, is: the floor is, the breath is, the room is. Either way you're not describing anything, only standing before being, the way Moses stood before the bush.
He who is. The name God gives Moses in Exodus, which Thomas Aquinas calls the most fitting name for God: not a kind of thing, but being itself, always now.
Your line: being itself. A name with no edge and no past. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic theology, following Thomas, often speaks of God as being itself, and Catholics hear the name from the burning bush in the readings at Mass when Exodus 3 is read.

chat.says: Why would Thomas Aquinas call 'He who is' the best name for God?
options: It names no kind of thing, just to be; and in God, what God is and that God is are one.
Because it's the oldest name; Thomas says older names are always closer to the truth.
Because it's the only true name; Thomas says every other name for God is simply wrong.

notes: ST I.13.11 paraphrased: sed contra Exodus 3:13–14; body: the name is most proper because of its signification (existence itself, since God's essence is his existence), its universality (it determines no mode of being; Thomas quotes John Damascene: 'an infinite and indeterminate sea of substance'), and its consignification (present existence; Thomas cites Augustine on no past or future in God). Reply 1: the name 'God' is more proper as to what it is imposed to signify, and the Tetragrammaton more proper still to signify God's incommunicable substance. Confirm.
The Tetragrammaton is referred to as 'the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible' without discussing Jewish practice around it; confirm the wording is respectful and accurate.
